context: process plant · electrolyser stacks, rectifiers, compression and storage; hazardous-area and purity tests

brief.intro: New to this project type? A green hydrogen plant splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using renewable electricity. Very pure water is fed to electrolyser stacks; large transformer-rectifiers supply them with direct current; the hydrogen that comes off is cooled, dried and purified, then compressed and stored in tubes or tanks, or piped on to a user such as an ammonia plant. Much of it is modular — stacks and skids arrive factory-built and are set in a hall or outdoors. But it is a real process plant: hydrogen is flammable and leaks easily, so piping is welded and tested to a high standard, areas are classified as hazardous, and detection, ventilation and venting are safety-critical. The big electrical supply and the electrolyser delivery are the long items; commissioning ends with a purity and performance test.

must_get_right: The power supply (connection, substation, rectifier-transformers) is as large as the process plant; put it at the front of the schedule.
Electrolyser stacks and rectifiers are the long-lead items and suppliers have limited capacity — the order date fixes the earliest start-up.
Hydrogen piping needs high-integrity welding, cleaning and helium or pressure leak testing; do not treat it as ordinary utility piping.
Safety systems (gas detection, ventilation, ESD) must be proven before hydrogen is introduced, and the offtake — pipeline, trailers or the downstream plant — must be ready to take the gas.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant unit (electrolysis, gas processing, compression and storage, utilities, power supply) and by system for commissioning.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; commissioning by system, with continuous operation during the performance test.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Engineering and HAZOP → long-lead orders → foundations and hall → equipment setting → piping and electrical → mechanical completion by system → leak tests → utilities commissioned → safety systems proven → purging → first hydrogen → purity → performance test. The critical path runs through the electrolyser or rectifier delivery, or the power connection.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Renewable or grid power is available at the required capacity for commissioning; water supply is available; the offtake (pipeline, trailers or downstream plant) is ready to accept hydrogen at first production.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Hazardous-area rules apply once hydrogen is on site; stacks are sensitive to contamination and must be stored and installed in clean, dry conditions.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: electrolyser delivery and supplier capacity, power-supply readiness, leaks at the tightness test, purity not reached at first start-up, and a late offtake. Contingency is held before first hydrogen.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant unit and system; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the mechanical, piping and commissioning teams — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
